meta.title: Drive: The Surprising Truth About What Motivates Us
meta.author: Daniel H. Pink

paragraphs.heading: Summary of Introduction
sentences: In the **1940s**, psychologist Harry F. Harlow conducted a groundbreaking but overlooked study on **rhesus monkeys**.
Harlow offered them puzzles without **rewards** like food or affection, yet they solved them with **enthusiasm**.
This behavior suggested a **third drive**—intrinsic motivation, a joy in the task itself.
Decades later, Edward Deci's experiments with participants confirmed Harlow's findings, revealing intrinsic motivation's power, especially compared to external rewards like **money**.
This led to new insights questioning our **understanding** of motivation, emphasizing the need to rethink approaches in **business** and education.

parts.title: Drive - Rethinking Motivation and Motivation Models

sentences: **Summary Chunk:**
**Economists Wrong About Motivation**: Economists predicted in 1995 that Microsoft's paid expert-led encyclopedia would trump the free, volunteer-contributed Wikipedia.
In **2009, Microsoft shut down Encarta** while Wikipedia became the world's largest encyclopedia.
Despite **expectations based on financial incentives**, volunteers created successful open-source platforms like Wikipedia and **Firefox**.
This challenges the traditional view that people work only for money.
**Shift from Old Motivational Models**: Historically, societies relied on a Motivation 2.0 model based on **"carrots and sticks,"** rewarding good behavior and punishing bad to drive performance.
However, **complexity and creativity**, not routine tasks, define today's economy.
Most of our economic theory was based on the assumption that humans **maximize wealth** and behave **rationally**.
Behavioral economics, pioneered by figures like **Daniel Kahneman**, shows humans act on a blend of economic and more **transcendental** motivations.
**Creativity and Intrinsic Motivation**: Modern work increasingly involves **heuristic tasks,** those requiring new solutions rather than following set rules.
Teresa Amabile's **Intrinsic Motivation Principle** suggests that creativity thrives not on extrinsic rewards but on **internal motivation.**
In a **flattening organizational world**, where jobs are more diverse and people often work remotely, old **extrinsic incentive models** fail.
**New business structures**, such as L3Cs and social businesses, focus on **purpose** beyond profit.
This **restructuring** indicates a shift towards needing **self-directed, inherently motivated people.**

parts.title: Reassessing Motivation 2.0: The Rise of Intrinsic Motivation

sentences: Motivation **2.0**, which relies on **external rewards** and **punishments**, was once seen as the ideal operating system for businesses.
This approach, dubbed the "carrot and stick" method, suggested that paying people more for their work would lead to **improved performance**.
The success of **Microsoft's Encarta** under this system was not uncommon in earlier times when many tasks were **algorithmic** and **routine**.
However, the abrupt success of **Wikipedia**, an **open-source model** driven by intrinsic motivation, challenged this traditional viewpoint.
This **success** was just one example of the flaws in Motivation **2.0**.
Humans are complex and not purely **rational**, which behavioral economics reveals.
We often act out of **emotion** and intrinsic factors rather than **financial gain**.
Moreover, many modern jobs have grown **creative** and **self-directed**, making the traditional carrot-and-stick approach less effective.
**Intrinsic rewards**, like the satisfaction of solving a problem or mastering a skill, often prove more motivating.

As such, **Motivation 2.0** falls short in today's world where tasks require **creativity**, leaders need people who are **self-motivated** rather than dependent on **external incentives**, and where new **business models** shirk traditional organizational structures.
Recognizing this challenge encourages a shift towards a new motivation system, one that accounts for people's **inherent human desires** for creativity, purpose, and autonomy.
***Newton's First Law*** tells us that an object will stay in motion until acted on by an outside force.
In motivation, similarly, **rewards** and **punishments** should actually help get more or less of a behavior, but often they **backfire**.
This is evident in many settings, from puzzles to office tasks, revealing strange outcomes that are counter to what we'd expect, much like in **quantum mechanics.**
***Baseline rewards*** like salary ensure basic needs are met, preventing **anxiety** and **distrust**.
But beyond that, using **carrots and sticks** can decrease motivation.
Acts of **creativity** can be stifled, and attempts to promote positive actions might make them vanish.
Instead of **reducing** undesirable behavior, sometimes, they promote it, risking **cheating** and **short-sightedness**.
Research like **Deci's Soma experiment** illustrates that expected rewards can lead to getting less of what we want.
This is supported by Tom Sawyer's story – where **work** and **play** are inversely related depending on **obligation**.
When something fun is rewarded with money, it is often stripped of its intrinsic joy, turning it into a chore.
This highlights how **external incentives** might undermine **intrinsic motivation**, which is crucial for **creativity** and integrity.
**Rewards** can **limit our thinking** in two major ways.
**Extrinsic motivators**, particularly the **if-then variety**, can cause us to focus only on **immediate, short-term goals**, rather than **long-term consequences**.
In some situations, concentrating solely on the immediate is understandable, but over time, **this fixation can be damaging**.
For instance, in **big companies**, the obsession with **quarterly earnings** can lead to **short-sighted decisions** that harm long-term innovation and growth.
**Short-term rewards** often **outweigh long-term costs**, potentially leading to unethical behaviors or **addictive patterns** seen in models like economic bubbles.
In contrast, there are circumstances where **extrinsic motivators** can be beneficial.
**Routine tasks** that require following a set of **specific instructions** can be enhanced by **small rewards** since they don’t harm **creativity**.
Take, for instance, a managerial context where a **dull task**, like preparing mail, requires some **extra nudge** for completion.
Here, offering **tangible rewards** like a **bonus or recognition** can help complete the task without undermining **intrinsic motivation**.
To use extrinsic rewards effectively, managers should also offer a **rationale** for the task, acknowledge its **mundane nature**, and give employees **autonomy** in their methods.
For more **creative, non-routine tasks**, it's best to avoid traditional rewards and focus on **understanding deeper motivation**.
Such as when producing a **creative poster**, offering a **monetary incentive** might restrict creativity.
Instead, fostering a climate of **autonomy, creative opportunity,** and a **sense of purpose** helps.
When rewards are unavoidable, they should be **unexpected** and occur **after task completion** to avoid damaging intrinsic drive.
Providing **informative feedback** and **praise** as rewards can enhance motivation without the caveats of **if-then rewards**.
**Deci and Ryan** have developed **self-determination theory (SDT)** suggesting three innate psychological needs: **competence, autonomy, and relatedness**.
When these needs are met, humans become motivated and productive, but when thwarted, they struggle.
They propose creating environments that nurture these needs instead of overusing rewards, which often demotivate.
They lead a strong academic network worldwide, revealing that fostering intrinsic motivation enhances productivity across various fields.

paragraphs.heading: Autonomy: A Key Driver of Motivation 3.0
sentences: One of the **main drivers** of motivation in the workplace, as well as in other areas, is **autonomy**.
Atlassian, a software company, has embraced this by allowing employees to spend 20% of their time on projects of their choosing.
This **freedom** has resulted in 48 new projects launched in one year, showcasing how essential **autonomy over tasks** is to creativity and satisfaction.
Such policies reflect the success of historical initiatives, like 3M's bootlegging policy, leading to innovations such as the Post-it note.
Despite the **proven results**, few companies adopt this method.
Google is an exception, transforming 20% time into successful products like Gmail and Google News.

The **billable hour** system in law firms exemplifies a lack of time autonomy, contrasting with companies like Best Buy that implement **Results-Only Work Environments** (ROWE) for more fulfillment and efficiency.
Freeing workers from strict constraints **enhances** intrinsic motivation and productivity.

paragraphs.heading: Wars and Realizations
sentences: At age ten, **Mihaly Csikszentmihalyi** experienced terrifying events, such as bombings and Nazi occupation, making him question if adults truly **knew how to live**.
This early brush with war led him to search for **better ways of living**.
His journey took him to drop out of school and seek answers through various European jobs.
A lecture by **Carl Jung** introduced him to psychology, setting him on a path to the United States to study and later make significant contributions.

paragraphs.heading: The Flow Phenomenon
sentences: Through his studies on **creativity** and **play**, Csikszentmihalyi discovered the concept of **autotelic experiences**, eventually naming it **flow**.
Flow describes when individuals are **fully absorbed**, finding the activity itself rewarding.

This insight came through observing **painters** and conducting extensive research with various individuals, understanding that optimal experiences involve activities where **challenges match skills**, leading to deep engagement.

paragraphs.heading: Applying Flow in Life and Work
sentences: Csikszentmihalyi's concept of flow suggests workplaces lack **engagement** and thus, mastery.
Instead, they often focus on **compliance**, missing out on the benefits of engaged, motivated individuals.
Companies like **Ericsson** have used flow principles to improve productivity, seeing results like **Green Cargo**, which became profitable thanks to focusing on **employee engagement**.
The idea is not just to complete tasks but to sculpt them to find **satisfaction**, suggesting a shift from seeing work as a chore to recognizing its **potential for joy**.
**Purpose and Boomers:** As the largest demographic cohort turns **sixty**, many boomers start questioning their **life's purpose**.

Their reflections on how swiftly time passed, the regrets they harbor, and wondering if they've made a **difference in the world** spark a collective **soul-searching** that's becoming increasingly common globally due to the large numbers hitting this milestone annually.
**Purpose-driven Motivation:** An emerging motivation framework, **Motivation 3.0**, combines **autonomy, mastery**, and most importantly, **purpose**.
It highlights a shift from **profit-maximizing** endeavors to those that also integrate **purpose maximization**, thereby offering more worker satisfaction.
This includes examples of ventures and organizations that place purpose on equal footing with profit, creating a new business ethos.
**Motivation Shift in Business:** Business philosophers advocate for **purpose maximization**, going beyond traditional profit motives.

There are observable shifts toward combining **intrinsic motivations** within organizations, as seen with initiatives like the **MBA Oath** for graduating students and **creative ventures** that defy conventional profit-centric models.
This shift suggests a more **holistic approach** to management and business goals, where **purpose** infuses activities with more profound **meaning and fulfillment**.

parts.title: Enhancing Autonomy and Motivation in Organizations

sentences: **Organizations** can encourage **innovation** and **autonomy** through initiatives like Kimley-Horn's peer-to-peer bonus system, where employees can instantly reward colleagues for exceptional performance, fostering a motivating environment.

Conducting an **Autonomy Audit** can help organizations assess the level of freedom employees actually experience in aspects such as tasks, time management, team selection, and methods, helping identify areas for improvement.
Leaders can adopt a **Type I** approach by relinquishing control, involving employees in goal setting, using non-controlling language, and holding office hours to encourage open communication.

parts.title: Innovative Work Concepts and Motivation Strategies

sentences: **Cali Ressler** and **Jody Thompson**, former **HR professionals** at **Best Buy**, introduced a radical new work concept called **ROWE** (Results-Only Work Environment).
In ROWE, **employees** enjoy **complete autonomy** in **when, where**, and **how** they work, focusing solely on results.
It eliminates schedules and emphasizes efficiency.
Learn more about it on their **website**.

**Gary Hamel**, a top business strategy expert and **professor** at **London Business School**, argues that **management** is outdated, likening it to an old technology that needs a complete overhaul.
He questions if workloads truly support **employee initiative** and passion and suggests reforms to better incentivize commitment.
**Type I Fitness Plan**: Encourages **autonomy** in exercise by setting personal, **intrinsic goals**.
It advises choosing enjoyable fitness activities to promote **mastery** and using **rewards** wisely.
The spirit of intrinsic motivation is explored, offering methods to integrate this drive outside work, enhancing **exercise motivation**.
